Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

SMSD 1.0.0

Release Preparation

  • Added two installed vignettes: replications of worked examples and new simulation rows from published sequential methods papers; and a study of coverage and sample size in difficult Pearson and multiple R-squared designs, with individual-study data, uncertainty intervals, and figures. Simulation caches record seeds and implementation fingerprints.
  • AIPE check displays and generated reports identify their confidence level as asymptotic, separately from satisfying the interval width criterion. The multiple R-squared help page and coverage vignette distinguish interior population values from the null boundary, where the normal approximation does not acquire nominal coverage with increasing n. A reproducible normal model reference calculation compares alternative intervals with fixed sample sizes that meet the coverage and width targets.
  • Fixed overflow in the standardized mean difference used by power_z() when opposite signed means have a finite difference in standard deviation units. Two-sided normal and t quantiles retain finite values at extreme valid confidence levels.
  • Rank correlation variance calculations use sorting and cumulative counts, with O(n log n) work and O(n) working memory, instead of quadratic comparisons or comparison matrices. Tied ranks retain the same formulas; the existing statistical warning about ties remains.
  • Added a site builder that renders a committed checkout, excluding ignored working notes. Continuous integration can run on preparation branches and on demand, and includes Windows R-devel.

First CRAN release. SMSD (“Sequential Methods for Study Design”) is for planning a study when the population values that a sample size formula needs (a standard deviation, a correlation, the effect size itself) are unknown. Data are collected in stages, and after each stage a stopping rule computed from the data in hand says whether sampling can stop. SMSD is the sequential companion of ‘DMAR’, which plans fixed sample sizes and is installed with it.

Every procedure has a *_pilot() function, which returns the pilot sample size, and a check function, which takes the data collected so far and evaluates the stopping rule once. The accuracy in parameter estimation procedures, the minimum risk procedures for the coefficient of variation and the standardized mean difference, and the budget procedure also have a *_sensitivity() function, which simulates the whole procedure for a planned design. The user owns the sampling loop: a check function does not prompt, print, or keep anything between calls.

The Procedures

A Narrow Confidence Interval for an Effect Size

  • Sequential accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE). Sampling stops at the first sample size that meets the stopping rule, and the confidence interval at that point is no wider than the requested full width. The standardized mean difference (seq_aipe_smd()), the coefficient of variation (seq_aipe_cv()), the simple linear regression slope (seq_aipe_reg_coef()), the standardized mean (seq_aipe_sm()), and a contrast of group means (seq_aipe_c()) follow Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243, doi:10.1037/met0000127). The Pearson, Kendall, and Spearman correlations (seq_aipe_r()) follow Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019, Psychological Methods, 24(4), 492–515, doi:10.1037/met0000203). The Gini index (seq_aipe_gini()) follows Chattopadhyay and De (2016, Econometrics, 4(3), 30, doi:10.3390/econometrics4030030). None of these assumes a particular distribution for the data.

  • The squared multiple correlation coefficient. seq_aipe_R2_pilot(), seq_aipe_R2(), and seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity() implement the procedure of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019, pp. 503–507), with the Wald interval (the default) or the log transformed interval of Bonett and Wright (2011). Unlike the other AIPE procedures, this one assumes multivariate normality. The procedure reproduces the article’s Tables 11 to 14. For the Wald interval the stopping rule uses (R2 + 1/n) * (1 - R2 + 1/n)^2, with 1/n added to both factors of the variance. Equation 63 as printed has (1 - (R2 + 1/n))^2 as its second factor, which does not reproduce the published tables and can leave the interval wider than the target. The help page documents the difference.

  • What is guaranteed, and what is not. Whenever a seq_aipe_* stopping rule is met, the interval is no wider than the target. Coverage is an asymptotic property under the relevant regularity conditions: it approaches the confidence level as the target narrows and the final sample grows, and it can fall well short in small samples. Each help page says so and reports what was measured for that effect size. Coverage at wide targets is below the confidence level for the Pearson correlation, the regression slope, and the coefficient of variation, and for any correlation when the association is strong; for the squared multiple correlation it falls badly when the sample is small relative to the number of predictors, and seq_aipe_R2() attaches a note whenever it reports an interval from fewer than p * max(20, 2 * p) observations. A narrower target or a larger minimum pilot sample (m_0) can help, and the sensitivity functions show what a planned design can expect. At the null multiple R-squared boundary, increasing n does not restore nominal Wald coverage; a different interval construction is needed.

  • The correction to Equation 26. The asymptotic variance of the standardized mean difference restores a factor of 1/2 that Equation 26 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018) omits. The two forms differ only when the means differ and the third central moments of the groups differ. The authors’ correction is installed with the package (system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD")), and ?seq_aipe_smd gives its web address.

  • seq_aipe_r() takes its paired data as x and y, like seq_aipe_reg_coef(). With method = "kendall" or "spearman" it warns when the data contain ties, because those variance estimators assume continuous data.

  • seq_aipe_c() requires balanced groups, as in Example 6 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018); criterion_n and current_n are per group. The unbalanced extension of the article (Equations 39 to 47) is not implemented.

  • seq_aipe_reg_coef() and seq_aipe_c() estimate quantities that have units, and their help pages have a Units paragraph: when the variables are recorded on a scale that makes the variance estimate tiny, a note says so and advises rescaling.

  • The point estimates gini_index(), gini_mean_diff(), and slr_slope() are exported for use on their own.

Minimum Risk Point Estimation

  • Minimum risk point estimation (MRPE). Sampling stops when the estimated risk, the cost of estimation error plus the cost of the observations, is as small as it can be made: seq_mr_cv() for the coefficient of variation (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2016, Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648, doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279) and seq_mr_smd() for the standardized mean difference (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2017, Psychological Methods, 22(1), 94–113, doi:10.1037/met0000089), each with its pilot function.

  • seq_mr_smd() takes one sampling cost c for the equal cost procedure (Equation 15 of the article) or c = c(c1, c2) for the article’s unequal cost procedure (“A General Scenario”, Equations 17 to 21). The rows next_n1 and next_n2 give the size each group should have at the next check, so the sampling loop is the same whichever group costs more. The article assumes normal populations with a common variance, and seq_mr_smd_sensitivity() shows what a skewed population costs. ?seq_mr_smd lists each point at which the function departs from the article as printed.

  • seq_mr_cv() has variance = c("corrected", "published"). The default is the estimator of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, Equations 30 to 32), which is consistent for any population with a finite fourth moment. "published" is Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016), offered so that the article’s worked example and tables, and DMAR::mr_cv(), can be reproduced. The two agree for normal data, and for any population with no excess kurtosis, and can differ otherwise. The derivation is installed with the package (system.file("cv_variance_note.md", package = "SMSD")).

  • seq_mr_cv_sensitivity() and seq_mr_smd_sensitivity() run a minimum risk procedure to its stopping point on simulated data and report the best fixed sample size and its risk, the distribution of the final sample size, the risk efficiency with its Monte Carlo standard error, and the regret.

A Budget Across Groups

  • A contrast under a fixed budget (Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal, 2025, Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439, doi:10.1037/met0000570). seq_budget_optimal() returns the optimal sample sizes of Theorem 1; seq_budget_pilot() returns the pilot size; seq_budget() evaluates the Equation 18 criterion on the data in hand; seq_budget_next() names the group that should receive the next observation; and seq_budget_sensitivity() simulates the whole procedure for a planned design.

  • seq_budget_next() never names a group the remaining budget cannot pay for, so a study that follows it one observation at a time cannot overspend. It returns NA when sampling has ended, and a sampling loop should end on that NA.

  • seq_budget() reports how sampling ended in three attributes: rule_met (every group reached its criterion), budget_exhausted (the budget cannot pay for another needed observation), and is_satisfied. Data that already cost more than the budget are flagged (budget_exceeded). By default every group is judged on the current data at each check; the closed argument, with order = "rounds" in seq_budget_next(), gives the package’s reading of the article’s first passage rule, and ?seq_budget_next lists the three details in which it differs from the article.

  • Four decisions, one family. decide_seq_budget_noninferiority(), decide_seq_budget_superiority(), decide_seq_budget_inferiority(), and decide_seq_budget_equivalence() are one-sided tests at alpha_level (default 0.05; two one-sided tests for equivalence), computed from the contrast estimate and its standard error as in the article and in DMAR::ss_seq_c(). None reads the two-sided interval stored on the check. The help states each null and alternative hypothesis in symbols and in words and the sign convention of each margin.

  • The help for the budget functions states how far coverage and the level of the tests fall short of nominal, by pilot size.

Classical Procedures for a Mean, a Median, or a Location

  • Procedures from Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009, Sequential methods and their applications, ISBN:9780367386535): fixed width confidence intervals (seq_fwd_norm_mean(), seq_fwd_dfr_mean(), seq_fwd_nexp_mean()), a bounded length interval for a median (seq_blci_dfr_median()), bounded risk point estimation (seq_br_norm_mean()), minimum risk point estimation (seq_mr_norm_mean(), seq_mr_exp_mean(), seq_mr_nexp_mean(), seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb()), and the two stage procedures (ts_fwd_norm_mean(), ts_fwd_dfr_mean(), ts_fwd_nexp_mean(), ts_br_norm_mean(), ts_br_exp_mean()), each with its pilot function.

  • Each help page says what is estimated (the *_nexp_mean functions estimate the location of a negative exponential distribution, not its mean), what d is in that procedure (a half width, a full width, or half the largest length allowed), every returned row and attribute, and whether the guarantee is exact or asymptotic, with the coverage or risk measured by simulation where it is asymptotic. Stein’s two stage interval for a normal mean (ts_fwd_norm_mean()) is exact; the distribution free two stage interval (ts_fwd_dfr_mean()) is asymptotic and falls short of its nominal level, and its help page gives the size of the shortfall.

  • seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal() gives the sample size for a fixed width interval for a normal mean when the variance is known, the benchmark the sequential procedures are compared with. power_z() gives the Type II error rate and the sample size of a one sample, one-sided z test.

Studying a Design Before Collecting Data

  • Every seq_aipe_* procedure, the contrast and the squared multiple correlation included, both minimum risk procedures, and the budget procedure have a *_sensitivity() function. Each runs the procedure from its pilot sample to its stopping point G times against a known data generating mechanism and returns a term/value summary of class smsd_sensitivity, which prints in fixed notation.

  • The seq_aipe_* and seq_mr_* sensitivity functions have batch = 1L, the number of observations added between checks of the stopping rule. The default is the purely sequential procedure of the articles; a larger value shows the overshoot to expect when a study can check only after every several observations. max_n is an exact cap for any batch size.

  • The AIPE summary has 13 rows, among them pct_hit_max_n, the percentage of replications that the cap stopped before the rule was met, and pct_variance_unusable, the percentage in which the variance estimate was unusable at one or more checks.

  • seed = NULL is the default everywhere. With a number the result is reproducible and the caller’s random number stream is left as it was found.

  • A true value at which the simulated data could not be used (for example a standardized mean difference of 1e8 or more, or a coefficient of variation of 1e-8 or less) is an error that names the argument, raised before anything is simulated.

Reading and Reporting a Result

  • The whole stopping path in one call. seq_path(check, data, ..., start = NULL, by = 1L) applies a sequential check function to data already in hand at each successive sample size and returns an smsd_path object: one row per stage and the first sample size at which the stopping rule is met (stop_n). It replaces the loop a user would otherwise write by hand, starts at the procedure’s pilot sample size by default, and has print(), format(), summary(), as.data.frame(), and plot() methods. The plot shows the estimate with its interval, and the current sample size against the criterion, at every stage.

  • The path shows what the rule would have said at each sample size. A sequential design reports the estimate at the first sample size at which the rule is met; the later stages are shown for illustration only, and the help page and the print method say so. All of the data go in data, and seq_path() stops when a second group or variable is passed outside it, where it would be seen in full from the first stage on. Data with missing values are refused. The two stage and budget procedures, which have no path indexed by one common sample size, are refused with advice.

  • A paragraph for the write-up. seq_report() turns a check or a path into a paragraph for a methods or results section: the procedure and its source, the target, the sample size at which the rule was met (or that it has not yet been met), and the estimate with its interval. The full reference is returned with it. For the budget procedure it says how sampling ended, and a spent budget is never reported as a stopping rule that was met.

What Every Check Function Shares

  • The object. A check function returns an object of class smsd_check: a data frame with the columns term and value. The stopping decision is attr(out, "is_satisfied"), which is always TRUE or FALSE, never NA; the method, the current and criterion sample sizes, the targets, and any notes are attributes as well. Stored values are never rounded.

  • Its methods. print(), format(), summary(), as.data.frame(), and methods for the tidy() and glance() generics of the ‘generics’ package. SMSD does not export those two generics: call generics::tidy(out) and generics::glance(out), or attach ‘generics’ or ‘broom’ first. tidy() uses the column layout of ‘DMAR’. Subsetting with [ returns a plain data frame whenever the result is no longer the complete check, so a partial object is never printed as a complete one.

  • An unusable variance estimate means the rule is not met. In a small sample the variance estimate that a stopping rule needs can be zero, negative, or not finite. The check then reports the rule as not met, sets attr(out, "variance_unusable") to TRUE, and attaches a note that print() shows, so sampling continues. This is a deliberate departure from the stopping rules as printed in the source articles. Under them a lower bound of n^-3 stands in for such an estimate and the rule is met at once, with an interval about a tenth of the requested width. At a target width of 0.4 that happened at the pilot sample in 14 percent of simulated studies of a Pearson correlation of 0.4 and in 16 percent of studies of a regression slope of 0.5. A positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe.

  • No variation is judged the same way everywhere. A sample whose values agree to ten significant digits is treated as having no variation, so scores that are equal on paper but differ by rounding error (gains of 0.3 computed as posttest minus pretest) are not taken for data with a tiny variance. In the purely sequential functions that estimate a variance or a scale, such a sample leaves the rule not met. (A predictor that does not vary is an error in seq_aipe_R2(), because the squared multiple correlation is then not defined.) In ts_fwd_norm_mean(), ts_fwd_dfr_mean(), ts_fwd_nexp_mean(), and ts_br_norm_mean() it is an error, because there the first stage variance or scale alone fixes the total sample size. Three functions estimate neither and are not affected: seq_blci_dfr_median(), where constant data give an interval of length zero and so meet the rule, and seq_mr_exp_mean() and ts_br_exp_mean(), whose rules use only the sample mean.

  • Results are right at any magnitude of the data. The seq_aipe_* variance estimators, gini_index(), gini_mean_diff(), slr_slope(), seq_mr_cv(), seq_mr_smd(), and the two stage fixed width rules lose no precision on any scale a double can hold. Data recorded at 1e-150 or 1e150 times their size give the same unit free effect size and the same stopping decision; an estimate that has units is rescaled with the data; and a two stage rule gives the same total sample size when its target is stated in the same units. (The slope and the contrast have units, and their stopping rules depend on the units in which the variables are recorded, as in the article; see the Units paragraphs of ?seq_aipe_reg_coef and ?seq_aipe_c.) Where a classical procedure cannot represent a variance at an extreme scale, it stops with a message that says to change the units. No result holds Inf or NaN: a sample size, a limit, or a risk too large to represent is an error whose message names the arguments to check.

  • Every argument is checked. A missing, non-finite, wrongly sized, or wrongly typed argument stops with a message that names the argument and says what was received. Counts such as m_0, G, max_n, and batch must be whole numbers.

  • One set of names. Arguments are in snake_case, the confidence level is always conf_level = 0.95, and the data arguments are x for one sample, group_1 and group_2 for two independent groups, x and y for paired variables, groups for several groups, and pilot_data and additional_data for the two stage procedures. Pilot functions take the method’s own arguments, then m_0, then gamma.

Corrections to Earlier Development Versions

These changed results relative to the development versions distributed on GitHub before this release.

  • seq_mr_smd() applies Equation 15 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017) exactly. Earlier versions placed the correction term inside the square root and stopped early (at 71 per group instead of 75 in the article’s worked example); a still earlier one divided the mean difference by the pooled variance where the pooled standard deviation belongs. The article’s worked example and its Tables 1 to 4 now reproduce. With two costs the function implements the article’s own procedure; Equations 18 and 42 are implemented with the squared term that the article’s first order conditions (Equation 41) give, where the article prints the first power.

  • seq_mr_cv(): earlier versions used the corrected variance estimator while citing Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016), so results for data that are not normal differed from the article and from DMAR::mr_cv() without explanation. The variance argument now makes the choice explicit.

  • The pilot sample sizes of the classical procedures follow one rule, max(m_0, ceiling(K^(1 / (1 + gamma)))), where K is the procedure’s criterion constant, with m_0 and gamma as arguments. Several earlier pilots equaled the optimal sample size at a unit scale, which was several times too large for data with a small standard deviation and no protection for data with a large one. The two stage pilots have larger default minimums (10 for ts_fwd_norm_mean_pilot() and ts_fwd_nexp_mean_pilot(), 30 for ts_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot(), 20 for ts_br_exp_mean_pilot()), because a very small first stage costs many times the optimal sample size or, for the distribution free interval, much of the coverage.

  • ts_fwd_norm_mean() and ts_fwd_dfr_mean() use the two-sided quantile for their two-sided intervals, as do the seq_fwd_* and seq_blci_* pilots. Earlier versions used the one-sided quantile, which at conf_level = 0.95 made the total sample size about 30 percent too small, and more than that for a small first stage in Stein’s procedure.

  • seq_mr_nexp_mean() uses the scale estimate to the power k in its stopping criterion and reports the risk at the current sample size; its location row is the sample minimum. The negative exponential pilots use the criterion’s own constant.

  • The classical stopping criteria round the criterion sample size up. Earlier versions truncated it, which declared the rule met one observation early.

  • seq_br_norm_mean() and ts_br_norm_mean() report the risk at the current sample size and compute their constants in closed form, so that the reported risk no longer sits a shade above the bound at the sample size the rule calls for, and ts_br_norm_mean() no longer fails for a first stage above 344 observations.

  • seq_blci_dfr_median() requires the smallest sample size at which an order statistic interval can reach the confidence level (6 observations at 95%). Earlier versions could stop at two observations. The confidence level holds at a fixed sample size; a check whose rule is met carries a note that the coverage of the sequential procedure is lower, and the help page gives the measured figures.

  • Constant data no longer satisfy the stopping rule of a procedure that estimates a variance or a scale. Earlier versions of seq_fwd_norm_mean(), seq_fwd_dfr_mean(), seq_fwd_nexp_mean(), seq_br_norm_mean(), seq_mr_norm_mean(), seq_mr_nexp_mean(), and seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb() reported an optimal sample size of 0 or 1 for such data and the rule as met, and seq_aipe_c() reported a met rule with an interval of zero width. seq_blci_dfr_median() and seq_mr_exp_mean() estimate no variance, and constant data can meet their rules, as before. seq_mr_exp_mean() now requires positive data.

  • seq_aipe_c() requires balanced groups. The removed unbalanced branch could report a satisfied stopping rule with an interval wider than requested.

  • The central moment estimators behind the variance estimates are computed on centered data. The earlier raw power sum forms lost precision when the mean was large relative to the standard deviation.

  • seq_aipe_r(): the Pearson procedure is defined when the sample covariance is exactly zero, as happens with ratings, and the Kendall and Spearman variance estimators are computed in exact arithmetic on the ranks, so that an estimate that is zero on paper is exactly zero. Perfectly discordant pairs under Kendall’s tau, and two dichotomous variables in exact opposition under Spearman’s rho, are therefore reported as not yet usable and not as a met rule.

  • seq_aipe_cv() and seq_mr_cv() report a sample whose mean is zero, negative, or positive only by rounding error (centered or standardized scores) as not yet estimable. Earlier versions could return a negative or an enormous coefficient of variation.

  • gini_index() and gini_mean_diff(): integer input no longer overflows, a missing value with na.rm = FALSE is an error and not a wrong number, negative data are an error for the Gini index, and the index can no longer exceed 1 through rounding.

  • seq_budget(): only the groups that still need observations count toward budget_exhausted; with unequal costs a check could previously sit at “not satisfied” with no affordable observation left. The superiority, inferiority, and equivalence decisions test at a one-sided level of 0.05 by default, where they previously read the two-sided interval on the check (a one-sided level of 0.025 on a 95 percent interval), and their margin arguments are margin, margin_lower, and margin_upper.

  • power_z() checks that mu_1 exceeds mu_0, returns the sample size as the smallest whole number whose Type II error rate is at most beta, and handles a very small beta.

  • The sensitivity functions grow each simulated sample one observation at a time unless batch says otherwise; pct_hit_max_n counts only replications that the cap stopped before the rule was met; and coverage and the percentage rows are formed from counts.

  • Renamed for accuracy: seq_blci_dfr_mean() is seq_blci_dfr_median() (it estimates a median); calculate_c() is seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal(variance, d, conf_level) and returns a whole sample size of at least 1; the data argument of the one sample classical procedures is x; seq_aipe_r() takes x and y; the pilot functions take m_0 before gamma; and the estimate rows of the standardized mean and the slope are named sm and reg_coef.

  • Functions of the earliest versions under their present names: seq_aipe_cor() is seq_aipe_r(), seq_aipe_slr_slope() is seq_aipe_reg_coef(), seq_aipe_std_mean() is seq_aipe_sm(), and seq_aipe_contrast() is seq_aipe_c(). power() and the three functions it called (sample_size(), type_two_calc(), and power_seq()) are power_z() with its method argument. The helper functions those versions exported (V2_contrast() and the other V2_* functions, mu3(), mu4(), mu13(), mu22(), mu31(), s(), chi_prob(), chi_prob_2(), and chi_prob_3()) are no longer exported.

  • ts_fwd_norm_mean(), ts_fwd_dfr_mean(), and ts_fwd_nexp_mean() no longer take gamma, which is an argument of their pilot functions. ts_br_exp_mean_pilot() takes the loss constant A as its first argument: ts_br_exp_mean_pilot(A, w, m_0 = 20, gamma = 1).

  • The interactive interface of the earliest versions (an alpha argument, a pilot = TRUE/FALSE switch, console messages, and lists with title cased names) is gone, with no deprecation shims. seq_ubdes_norm() was removed; seq_budget() covers the design it was meant for. The package no longer needs the copula, matrixStats, or MASS packages.

Held Back for a Later Version

  • seq_mr_dfr_mean(), ts_mr_dfr_mean(), and their pilot functions are not part of this release. Whether their known lower bound is a bound on the standard deviation or on the variance, and how it should set the first stage size, could not be confirmed against Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009). seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb(), which places no restriction on the variance, remains.

  • prob_gn(), prob_hn(), prob_kn(), and seven_1() are not part of this release either. They could not be checked against Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009), and they return once they have been.

Documentation

  • Vignettes: introduction, the overview; step-by-step-sequential-workflow, one study followed from its pilot sample to its stopping point; complete-tour, the procedures one by one, with a cached simulation study of coverage and sample size; seq-aipe-smd and seq-aipe-correlations; mrpe-cv and mrpe-smd, which reproduce the published worked examples; seq-budget; sensitivity-analysis; and special-cases-and-simulation, on the classical procedures.

  • The package website adds a validation article (vignettes/articles/validation.Rmd in the source repository), which sets the package’s results beside the published tables.

  • citation("SMSD") gives the package and the six articles whose methods it implements, and the same metadata is in CITATION.cff.
